summary.title: Simplifying ARM Concurrency: Multicopy-atomic Axiomatic and Operational Models for ARMv8
summary.one_liner: Learn why ARMv8 dropped non-multicopy-atomic memory visibility in favour of a simpler multicopy-atomic model, and how its axiomatic and operational formalisations were proven equivalent.
takeaways: ARMv8 was revised from a non-multicopy-atomic model to a multicopy-atomic one, because the non-multicopy-atomic behaviour was not exploited in production and complicated other features.
The paper defines two formal concurrency models, an operational one (a simplification of the Flowing model) and the axiomatic model of the revised ARMv8 specification, and proves them equivalent.
The operational model is integrated into an executable exploration tool with a web interface, used to exhaustively check litmus tests.
The tool was demonstrated on a loop-unrolled Linux kernel lock implementation, a known speculation bug, and a fixed version.
summary.summary: This POPL 2018 paper by Pulte, Flur, Deacon, French, Sarkar and Sewell explains why ARMv8's relaxed memory model was simplified to be multicopy-atomic and gives the reasoning behind dropping the earlier non-multicopy-atomic option. It also includes more straightforward notions of dependency and a formal concurrency model in the architecture. The authors define an operational model (a simplified Flowing/Flat model) and the revised axiomatic model, and prove they are equivalent. The operational model is implemented in an executable exploration tool with a web interface, which is used to check a loop-unrolled Linux kernel lock, a known speculation bug, and a fixed version. The page also links to the Herd model, litmus tests and the equivalence proof.
